Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
Going out at night or being outside after dark

issues.item: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
issues.explanation: These three maladaptive strategy items do not form a clinically coherent set on their own. 'Avoid Dreams' and 'Avoid Physical Stress' are trauma-linked avoidance strategies, but 'Compulsive Cleaning' reflects a distinct control/ritualising pattern that is not clearly tied to the same military PTSD presentation in the absence of any supporting trigger, threat, memory, or appraisal items. With no active edges in the formulation, the node should still be internally coherent; here the items suggest different mechanisms (nightmare avoidance, bodily arousal avoidance, and compulsive control rituals) without evidence they belong to the same symptom pattern.

vignette:
Layla was nineteen when the mortar round hit her forward operating base in Helmand Province. She had been a communications specialist, assigned to a reinforced bunker that doubled as a relay station. The first explosion deafened her; the second collapsed a section of the sandbag wall and pinned a soldier beneath a beam. For the next three hours she crouched beside him, pressing a field dressing to his thigh while he faded in and out of consciousness. She remembers the sound of his breathing, the weight of debris against her back, and the certainty that they would not make it. They did make it-he was evacuated, she was pulled out after the all-clear-but something in her changed that night. She finished her deployment mechanically and left the service two months later, at twenty, with a recommendation for a database administration program.

Now, at twenty-one, Layla works as a DBA for a mid-sized logistics company. She lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment in a suburb that feels safe enough. She has built her life around a set of rules she never consciously decided on.

Layla avoids any situation that puts her body under physical stress. She takes the elevator even for a single flight of stairs. In the data center where she sometimes works, she refuses to carry server racks or climb ladders, always asking a colleague to handle the lifting. She drives to the grocery store two blocks away because walking makes her heart race, and the feeling of being out of breath reminds her of the dust and pressure in the bunker. She canceled her gym membership the week she moved into the apartment and has not exercised since.

At home and at work, Layla cleans and organizes things repeatedly to feel in control. Her desk at the office is spotless-keyboard aligned with the monitor, cables tied with Velcro straps, a single pen exactly parallel to the notepad. She wipes down the surfaces three times a day with disinfectant wipes. At home, she vacuums the living room every evening, folds her clothes into precise rectangles, and rearranges the items on her bathroom counter if they shift by even an inch. If someone moves one of her possessions, she becomes restless until she restores the order. The cleaning gives her a quiet sense of certainty that nothing else provides.

Layla never goes out at night. She leaves work by four-thirty, before the winter sun sets, and has her groceries delivered rather than shop after dark. She declined a promotion that would have required occasional after-hours support calls, and she has not seen her friends for dinner in over a year because they tend to meet at seven or eight. She does not answer the door after dusk and keeps all her blinds drawn once the streetlights come on. When she needs milk or bread on a late afternoon, she plans the trip carefully so she is home before the last light fades.

These rules have made her life narrow but manageable. She gets by. She notices that her colleagues find her habits odd-the cleaning, the early departures, the refusal to help with physical tasks-and she has stopped trying to explain. What brought her to seek help was the growing loneliness: a birthday she spent alone, a sister's wedding she left before the reception started. Layla is not sure she can give up the routines, but she is beginning to fear what will happen if she keeps them.
